meta: Why do two apps using the same AI model end up so different, one you use daily and one you delete after a try? The model is just the engine. An AI product also needs fuel, a steering wheel, brakes and a dashboard.

muc.title: Same model, two different fates
muc.text: Two apps use the same AI model. One you use every day, the other you delete after one try. Why? Because the model is just the engine.

muc.title: An engine isn't a car
muc.text: A good engine isn't a car yet. To drive, you also need fuel, a steering wheel, brakes and a dashboard. An AI product is the same.

muc.title: Your own data
muc.text: The fuel is your own data. A bakery's chatbot has to know that bakery's menu, prices and opening hours, not just general knowledge from the internet.

muc.title: The interface
muc.text: The steering wheel is the interface: buttons, suggested questions, a place to show results. A good interface helps people know what to ask, and what to do with the answer.

muc.title: Guardrails
muc.text: The brakes are guardrails: things AI must not say or do. The bakery chatbot must not promise discounts on its own, or chat about unrelated topics.

muc.title: Feedback from users
muc.text: And the dashboard: like and dislike buttons, questions people have to ask twice. It tells the product team whether the car is running well, or where it's about to break.

muc.title: Where's the difference?
muc.text: Many companies can rent the same engine. What makes the difference is the other four parts.

muc.title: Check an AI app you use
muc.text: Open an AI app you use often and ask yourself: what does it know about my own work? What does it block? Does it let me rate its answers? You'll see where it's strong and weak.

muc.title: Does this task even need AI?
muc.text: But before building the car, there's a bigger question: does this task really need AI? See you in part 2.
